FIN-01.Stocks: Shares of ownership in a company. Their value rises and falls with how the company and the market are doing.
FIN-01.Bonds: Loans an investor makes to a company or government. The borrower pays interest and returns the amount borrowed on a set date.
FIN-01.Real estate: Land and buildings bought to earn rent or to sell later at a higher price.
FIN-01.Mutual funds: Pools of money from many investors that a professional manager uses to buy a mix of stocks, bonds or other assets.
FIN-01.Cryptocurrency: Digital money, such as Bitcoin, recorded on a shared online ledger instead of being issued by a government. Its price can swing sharply.
FIN-01.ETFs: Exchange-traded funds hold a basket of investments, like a mutual fund, but their shares trade on a stock exchange all day like a single stock.
FIN-01.Index funds: Funds built to copy a market index, such as the S&P 500, by holding the same investments. They usually charge low fees.
FIN-01.Certificates of deposit: Bank deposits locked in for a fixed time at a fixed interest rate. Taking the money out early usually costs a penalty.
FIN-01.Savings account: A bank account that pays interest on money you leave in it. It is very safe but usually earns less than other investments.
FIN-01.Retirement account: An account such as a 401(k) or IRA (individual retirement account) that gives tax advantages for saving and investing money for retirement.
FIN-01.Commodities: Raw materials such as gold, oil or wheat. Investors buy them, or contracts based on them, hoping the price will rise.
FIN-01.Treasury bills: Short-term loans to the U.S. government that mature in a year or less. They are sold below face value and are considered very safe.
FIN-01.Options: Contracts that give the right, but not the duty, to buy or sell an asset at a set price by a set date. They are a kind of derivative.
FIN-01.Savings bonds: Bonds the U.S. government sells directly to individuals. They earn interest over many years and cannot be traded to other investors.
FIN-01.Money market account: A bank savings account that often pays a higher rate and may allow a few checks. A money market fund is a similar low-risk mutual fund.
FIN-01.Collectibles: Physical items such as art, coins or trading cards, bought in the hope they become rarer and more valuable over time.
FIN-01.Preferred stock: A class of company shares that pays a fixed dividend before common shareholders get anything, but usually carries no voting rights.
FIN-01.Municipal bonds: Bonds issued by states, cities or school districts to pay for public projects. The interest is often free of federal income tax.
FIN-01.Hedge funds: Private investment funds for wealthy investors and institutions. They use riskier strategies, such as borrowing and betting on prices falling.
FIN-01.Private equity: Money invested in companies that are not traded on a stock exchange, including venture capital for young startups.
FIN-01.Foreign currency: Money of another country, bought in the hope that its exchange rate will rise against your own currency.
FIN-01.Annuities: Contracts, usually with an insurance company, where you pay in money now and receive regular payments later, often during retirement.
FIN-01.REITs: Real estate investment trusts are companies that own income-producing property. Buying their shares lets you invest in real estate without owning a building.
FIN-01.Target-date funds: Funds built around a planned retirement year. They hold more stocks early on and shift toward safer bonds as that year gets closer.

FIN-02.Return on investment: The gain from an investment divided by what it cost, shown as a percentage. It tells you how much you earned for each dollar put in.
FIN-02.Profit margin: Profit divided by sales revenue. It shows how many cents of each sales dollar the business keeps as profit.
FIN-02.Price-to-earnings ratio: A stock's share price divided by the company's earnings per share. It shows how much investors pay for each dollar of profit.
FIN-02.Current ratio: Current assets divided by current liabilities. It shows whether a business can pay the bills due within the next year.
FIN-02.Debt-to-equity ratio: Total liabilities divided by owners' equity. It compares how much of the business is funded by borrowing with how much is funded by owners.
FIN-02.Return on equity: Net income divided by shareholders' equity. It shows how much profit a company earns on the money its owners have invested.
FIN-02.Earnings per share: Net income divided by the number of common shares outstanding. It shows how much profit belongs to each share.
FIN-02.Debt-to-income ratio: A person's monthly debt payments divided by monthly gross income. Lenders use it to judge whether a borrower can afford another loan.
FIN-02.Quick ratio: Cash, short-term investments and receivables divided by current liabilities. It is a stricter test than the current ratio because it leaves out inventory.
FIN-02.Return on assets: Net income divided by total assets. It shows how well a company turns everything it owns into profit.
FIN-02.Debt ratio: Total liabilities divided by total assets. It shows what share of a company's assets was paid for with borrowed money.
FIN-02.Dividend yield: The yearly dividend per share divided by the share price. It shows the cash return an investor gets from dividends alone.
FIN-02.Inventory turnover: Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. It shows how many times a business sells and replaces its stock in a period.
FIN-02.Asset turnover: Sales revenue divided by average total assets. It shows how many dollars of sales a company produces from each dollar of assets.
FIN-02.Accounts receivable turnover: Credit sales divided by average accounts receivable. It shows how many times a year a business collects what customers owe it.
FIN-02.Dividend payout ratio: Dividends divided by net income. It shows what share of profit is paid to shareholders and what share is kept in the business.
FIN-02.Price-to-book ratio: Share price divided by book value per share, which is equity per share on the balance sheet. It compares market value with accounting value.
FIN-02.Cash ratio: Cash and cash equivalents divided by current liabilities. It is the strictest liquidity test, counting only money on hand.
FIN-02.Interest coverage ratio: Operating earnings before interest and taxes divided by interest expense. It shows how many times over a company can pay its interest.
FIN-02.Days sales outstanding: Accounts receivable divided by average daily credit sales. It gives the average number of days customers take to pay.
FIN-02.Debt service coverage ratio: Operating income divided by the loan payments due, both principal and interest. Above 1 means the business earns enough to cover its debt payments.
FIN-02.Price-to-sales ratio: A company's market value divided by its yearly sales revenue. It shows how much investors pay for each dollar of sales.

FIN-03.Bank: A business that holds deposits, makes loans and handles payments for people and companies.
FIN-03.Credit union: A not-for-profit lender owned by its members. It offers the same basic services as a bank, often with lower fees and loan rates.
FIN-03.Investment bank: A firm that helps companies and governments raise money by selling stocks and bonds, and advises them on mergers and takeovers.
FIN-03.Insurance company: A firm that collects premiums from many customers and pays out when a covered loss happens. It invests the premiums in the meantime.
FIN-03.Brokerage: A firm that buys and sells stocks, bonds and other investments on behalf of its customers.
FIN-03.Savings and loan: An institution, also called a thrift, that takes savings deposits and focuses on lending for home mortgages.
FIN-03.Central bank: A nation's main monetary authority, such as the Federal Reserve. It manages the money supply, influences interest rates and oversees banks.
FIN-03.Hedge fund: A private investment fund open mainly to wealthy investors and institutions. It uses aggressive strategies to try to earn high returns.
FIN-03.Venture capital firm: A firm that invests in young companies with high growth potential in exchange for part ownership.
FIN-03.Mortgage company: A lender that specializes in home loans. Unlike a bank, it usually does not take deposits.
FIN-03.Credit card company: A business that issues credit cards, lends cardholders the money for purchases and earns interest and fees.
FIN-03.Private equity firm: A firm that raises money from investors to buy whole companies, improve them and sell them later for a profit.
FIN-03.Payday lender: A business that makes small, short-term loans due on the borrower's next payday. The fees make these loans very expensive.
FIN-03.Mutual fund company: A firm that pools money from many investors into funds and manages those funds for a fee.
FIN-03.Finance company: A lender that makes loans to consumers and businesses, such as car or furniture loans, but does not accept deposits.
FIN-03.Pension fund: A pool of money set aside by an employer or union and invested to pay workers' retirement benefits.
FIN-03.Trust company: A firm that manages money and property on behalf of others, such as the assets left in a trust or an estate.
FIN-03.Pawnshop: A shop that lends cash against a valuable item left as security. If the loan is not repaid, the shop sells the item.
FIN-03.Check-cashing service: A storefront business that turns paychecks and other checks into cash for a fee, often used by people without a bank account.
FIN-03.International financial institution: An organization owned by many countries, such as the World Bank or the International Monetary Fund, that lends to governments.

PFL-01.Health insurance: Coverage that pays part of the cost of doctor visits, hospital stays and prescriptions.
PFL-01.Auto insurance: Coverage for damage and injuries from car accidents, including harm you cause to others. Nearly every state requires drivers to carry it.
PFL-01.Life insurance: A policy that pays a sum of money to the people you name if you die, helping replace your income for your family.
PFL-01.Homeowners insurance: Coverage for a house and the belongings in it against fire, theft and storms, plus injuries to visitors on the property.
PFL-01.Renters insurance: Coverage for a tenant's belongings and liability. The landlord's policy covers the building but not what the renter owns.
PFL-01.Dental insurance: Coverage that helps pay for cleanings, fillings and other dental care.
PFL-01.Vision insurance: Coverage that helps pay for eye exams, glasses and contact lenses.
PFL-01.Property insurance: A broad term for coverage that pays when buildings or belongings are damaged, destroyed or stolen.
PFL-01.Disability insurance: A policy that replaces part of your income if illness or injury leaves you unable to work.
PFL-01.Liability insurance: Coverage that pays when you are legally responsible for injuring someone or damaging their property.
PFL-01.Pet insurance: Coverage that helps pay veterinary bills when a pet is sick or injured.
PFL-01.Travel insurance: Coverage for trip problems such as cancellations, lost luggage or a medical emergency away from home.
PFL-01.Business insurance: Policies that protect a company against losses such as property damage, lawsuits and interrupted operations.
PFL-01.Flood insurance: Separate coverage for flood damage, which standard homeowners policies normally do not include.
PFL-01.Long-term care insurance: A policy that helps pay for extended help with daily living, such as a nursing home or a home health aide.
PFL-01.Workers compensation: Insurance employers carry that pays medical costs and lost wages for employees who are hurt or made ill by their job.
PFL-01.Earthquake insurance: Separate coverage for earthquake damage, which standard homeowners policies normally leave out.
PFL-01.Unemployment insurance: A government program, funded mainly by taxes on employers, that pays temporary income to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.
PFL-01.Motorcycle insurance: Coverage for accidents, damage and liability involving a motorcycle, similar to auto insurance.
PFL-01.Malpractice insurance: Liability coverage for professionals such as doctors and lawyers, protecting them if a client claims their mistake caused harm.
PFL-01.Phone insurance: Coverage that repairs or replaces a mobile phone that is lost, stolen or damaged.
PFL-01.Umbrella insurance: Extra liability coverage that starts paying once the limits on your home and auto policies are used up.
PFL-01.Title insurance: A policy bought when purchasing property that protects the buyer or lender if someone else later proves a claim to ownership.
PFL-01.Boat insurance: Coverage for damage to a boat and for injuries or damage the boat's owner causes to others.
PFL-01.Mortgage insurance: Insurance a home buyer with a small down payment pays for. It protects the lender, not the buyer, if the loan is not repaid.
PFL-01.Deposit insurance: Government-backed protection for money in bank accounts, up to a limit, if the bank fails. In the U.S. the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) provides it.
PFL-01.Cyber insurance: Coverage for losses from hacking, data breaches and other computer attacks.
PFL-01.Crop insurance: Coverage farmers buy against losing a harvest to weather or disease, or against a drop in crop prices.
PFL-01.Accidental death and dismemberment: A policy that pays if the insured person dies or loses a limb, sight or hearing in an accident. It does not cover death from illness.

PFL-02.Payment history: Your record of paying bills and loans on time. It carries the most weight, so late or missed payments hurt a score the most.
PFL-02.Credit utilization: The share of your available credit that you are using, such as card balances compared with card limits. Lower use helps your score.
PFL-02.Length of credit history: How long your accounts have been open. A longer track record gives lenders more evidence of how you handle credit.
PFL-02.New credit: How many accounts you recently opened or applied for. Several applications in a short time can lower a score for a while.
PFL-02.Credit mix: The variety of credit you have, such as credit cards, a car loan and a student loan. Handling different kinds well helps a little.

PFL-03.Federal income tax: Money your employer holds back from each paycheck and sends to the U.S. government toward your yearly income tax bill.
PFL-03.Gross pay: Total earnings for the pay period before any taxes or other deductions are taken out.
PFL-03.Net pay: The amount you actually receive after all taxes and deductions are subtracted from gross pay. Also called take-home pay.
PFL-03.Social Security: A payroll tax taken from each paycheck that funds retirement, disability and survivor benefits. Your employer pays a matching amount.
PFL-03.Deductions: Amounts subtracted from gross pay, such as taxes, insurance premiums and retirement contributions.
PFL-03.Medicare: A payroll tax taken from each paycheck that funds the federal health insurance program for older Americans.
PFL-03.State income tax: Money withheld from your pay for your state's income tax. A few states have no income tax, so this line does not appear there.
PFL-03.Health insurance: Your share of the premium for an employer's health plan, taken out of each paycheck.
PFL-03.401(k) contribution: Money you choose to have taken from your pay and put into an employer retirement savings plan, often before income tax is figured.
PFL-03.Pay period: The span of dates the paycheck covers, such as one week, two weeks or a month.
PFL-03.Pay rate: How much you earn per hour, or your salary for the period. For hourly workers it is multiplied by hours worked to get gross pay.
PFL-03.Employee or employer name: Identifying details at the top of the stub showing who is being paid and which company is paying.
PFL-03.FICA: The Federal Insurance Contributions Act tax. It is the combined Social Security and Medicare tax withheld from wages.
PFL-03.Overtime: Extra pay for hours worked beyond the standard week, usually at one and a half times the regular hourly rate.
PFL-03.Hours worked: The number of hours you worked in the pay period, used to calculate an hourly worker's pay.
PFL-03.Regular pay: Earnings for normal hours at your normal rate, before any overtime, bonus or other extra pay is added.
PFL-03.Dental or vision insurance: Your share of the premiums for dental and eye-care plans offered by the employer, taken out of each paycheck.
PFL-03.Year-to-date totals: Running totals of your earnings, taxes and deductions from the start of the year up to this paycheck.
PFL-03.Union dues: Membership fees for a labor union, which the employer may take from your pay and pass on to the union.
PFL-03.Health savings account: Money set aside from your pay, before tax, into an account used for medical costs. A flexible spending account works in a similar way.
PFL-03.Local income tax: Tax withheld for a city, county or school district that charges its own income tax. Only some places have one.
PFL-03.Bonus or commission: Extra earnings on top of regular pay. A bonus rewards performance, and a commission is a percentage of the sales you make.
PFL-03.Paid time off: Hours of vacation or sick leave you have earned, used or have left. You are paid for these hours without working them.
PFL-03.Garnishment: Money an employer is legally ordered to take from your pay and send to someone you owe, such as for unpaid debts or child support.
PFL-03.Life insurance: The premium for life insurance offered through your employer, taken out of each paycheck if you pay part of the cost.
PFL-03.Disability insurance: A deduction for coverage that replaces part of your income if you cannot work. Some states run their own required program.
PFL-03.Withholding allowances: Entries from your Form W-4, such as filing status, that tell the employer how much income tax to hold back. Older forms used a number of allowances, which the current federal form no longer asks for.

ACC-01.Revenue: The total amount a business earns from selling goods or services in the period. It is the first line of the statement.
ACC-01.Net income: What is left after every expense and tax is subtracted from revenue. If the result is negative it is a net loss.
ACC-01.Expenses: The costs of running the business during the period, such as wages, rent and utilities. They are subtracted from revenue.
ACC-01.Cost of goods sold: The direct cost of the products that were sold in the period, such as what a store paid for the merchandise.
ACC-01.Gross profit: Revenue minus cost of goods sold. It shows what is left to cover operating expenses before they are subtracted.
ACC-01.Salaries and wages expense: What the business paid, or owes, its employees for work done during the period.
ACC-01.Taxes: The income tax the business owes on the period's profit. It is subtracted near the bottom of the statement.
ACC-01.Operating income: Gross profit minus operating expenses. It shows profit from the main business before interest and income taxes.
ACC-01.Rent expense: The cost of using buildings or space the business does not own, for the period covered.
ACC-01.Advertising expense: What the business spent during the period promoting its products and services.
ACC-01.Selling, general and administrative expe: Operating costs not tied directly to making the product, such as sales staff, office salaries and head office costs.
ACC-01.Interest expense: The cost of borrowing money during the period. It is usually listed below operating income.
ACC-01.Earnings per share: Net income divided by the number of common shares. Corporations report it at the bottom of the income statement.
ACC-01.EBITDA: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. It is a rough measure of profit from operations before those four items.
ACC-01.Income before taxes: Profit after all operating costs and interest, but before income tax is subtracted.
ACC-01.Utilities expense: The cost of electricity, water, gas and similar services used during the period.
ACC-01.Insurance expense: The cost of the insurance coverage that applied to this period.
ACC-01.Research and development: Money spent on creating new products or improving existing ones. Under U.S. accounting rules it is generally recorded as an expense in the period it is spent.
ACC-01.Depreciation: The portion of a long-lived asset's cost charged as an expense this period. Amortization does the same for intangible assets.
ACC-01.Sales returns and allowances: Refunds and price reductions given to customers. They are subtracted from gross sales to arrive at net sales.
ACC-01.Other income: Money earned outside the main business, such as interest on a bank account or a gain on selling old equipment.
ACC-01.Supplies expense: The cost of supplies, such as paper and cleaning products, that were used up during the period.

ACC-02.Cash: Money the business has on hand and in bank accounts. It is listed first among the assets because it is the most liquid.
ACC-02.Assets: Everything of value the business owns or controls, such as cash, inventory and equipment.
ACC-02.Liabilities: What the business owes to others, such as loans, unpaid bills and wages due.
ACC-02.Accounts receivable: Money customers owe the business for goods or services they bought on credit. It is an asset.
ACC-02.Inventory: Goods the business holds for sale to customers, plus any materials used to make them. It is a current asset.
ACC-02.Accounts payable: Money the business owes suppliers for goods or services bought on credit. It is a current liability.
ACC-02.Current assets: Cash and other assets expected to be turned into cash or used up within a year, such as receivables and inventory.
ACC-02.Equipment: Long-lived physical items used to run the business, such as machinery, vehicles and computers.
ACC-02.Owner's equity: The owners' stake in the business. It equals total assets minus total liabilities.
ACC-02.Long-term debt: Loans and other borrowings that do not have to be repaid within the next year.
ACC-02.Current liabilities: Debts the business must pay within a year, such as accounts payable and wages owed.
ACC-02.Retained earnings: The total profit a corporation has kept in the business over its life instead of paying it out as dividends. Part of equity.
ACC-02.Notes payable: Amounts owed under a signed written promise to repay, usually with interest, such as a bank loan.
ACC-02.Common stock: The ordinary ownership shares a corporation has issued, usually recorded at their par value. It is part of stockholders' equity.
ACC-02.Land: Ground the business owns. Unlike buildings, land is not depreciated because it does not wear out.
ACC-02.Supplies: Items such as paper and cleaning products bought for use in the business and not yet used. They count as a current asset.
ACC-02.Prepaid expenses: Costs paid in advance, such as insurance or rent for future months. They are assets until the benefit is used up.
ACC-02.Goodwill: An intangible asset recorded when a company buys another business for more than the fair value of its identifiable net assets.
ACC-02.Accrued liabilities: Expenses the business has already run up but not yet paid or been billed for, such as wages earned by staff before payday.
ACC-02.Short-term investments: Stocks, bonds and similar holdings the business plans to turn back into cash within a year.
ACC-02.Intangible assets: Valuable things with no physical form, such as patents, trademarks and copyrights.
ACC-02.Wages payable: Pay that employees have earned but the business has not yet handed over. It is a current liability.
ACC-02.Taxes payable: Taxes the business owes to the government but has not yet paid.
ACC-02.Bonds payable: Money a company owes to investors who bought its bonds. It is usually a long-term liability.
ACC-02.Mortgage payable: The unpaid balance on a loan that is secured by the business's land or buildings.
ACC-02.Notes receivable: Amounts others owe the business under a signed written promise to pay, usually with interest. It is an asset.
ACC-02.Accumulated depreciation: The total depreciation recorded on an asset since it was bought. It is subtracted from the asset's cost on the balance sheet.
ACC-02.Deferred revenue: Cash received from customers for goods or services not yet delivered. It is a liability until the business does the work.
ACC-02.Additional paid-in capital: The amount shareholders paid for stock above its par value, the small face amount printed on each share. Part of equity.
ACC-02.Treasury stock: A company's own shares that it has bought back from investors. It is subtracted from stockholders' equity.
ACC-02.Interest payable: Interest on loans that has built up but has not yet been paid. It is a current liability.
ACC-02.Allowance for doubtful accounts: An estimate of the customer debts that will never be collected. It is subtracted from accounts receivable.

ACC-03.Journalize transactions: Record each transaction in the journal in date order, showing which accounts are debited and credited.
ACC-03.Prepare financial statements: Use the adjusted account balances to produce the income statement, balance sheet and other reports for the period.
ACC-03.Post to the ledger: Copy each journal entry into the individual accounts in the ledger so every account shows its running balance.
ACC-03.Trial balance: A list of every account and its balance, prepared to check that total debits equal total credits.
ACC-03.Analyze transactions: The first step: look at source documents such as receipts and invoices to decide which accounts each transaction affects.
ACC-03.Adjusting entries: Entries made at the end of the period to record revenue earned and expenses used that have not yet been recorded, such as depreciation.
ACC-03.Closing entries: Entries that reset revenue, expense and dividend or drawing accounts to zero and move the period's profit into equity.
ACC-03.Adjusted trial balance: A second list of account balances, prepared after adjusting entries, used to build the financial statements.
ACC-03.Worksheet: An optional working paper with columns for the trial balance, adjustments and statements, used to organize figures before reporting.
ACC-03.Post-closing trial balance: A final check after the closing entries. Only asset, liability and equity accounts remain, and debits must still equal credits.
ACC-03.Reversing entries: Optional entries on the first day of a new period that undo certain adjusting entries, making later bookkeeping simpler.

FIN-04.Return on investment: The profit a project is expected to earn divided by what it costs. A higher percentage means more gain for each dollar spent.
FIN-04.Payback period: The number of years it takes for a project's cash inflows to repay the original cost. Shorter is safer, but it ignores later cash.
FIN-04.Net present value: The value in today's dollars of all a project's future cash flows, minus its cost. A positive result means the project adds value.
FIN-04.Cost-benefit analysis: A comparison of everything a project is expected to cost with everything it is expected to gain, to see if the benefits are larger.
FIN-04.Internal rate of return: The discount rate at which a project's net present value is exactly zero. The project is accepted if this rate beats the required return.
FIN-04.Break-even analysis: A calculation of how many units or sales dollars a project needs before its revenue covers all its costs.
FIN-04.Accounting rate of return: A project's average yearly accounting profit divided by the amount invested. It is simple but ignores the time value of money.
FIN-04.Cash flow analysis: A forecast of the cash a project will bring in and pay out each period, to see whether and when it produces spare cash.
FIN-04.Feasibility study: An early investigation of whether a project is practical and likely to pay off, covering costs, demand and risks.
FIN-04.Profitability index: The present value of a project's future cash flows divided by its initial cost. A result above 1 means the project is worth more than it costs.
FIN-04.Discounted payback period: The time a project takes to repay its cost when future cash flows are first reduced to today's dollars.
FIN-04.Sensitivity analysis: A test that changes one assumption at a time, such as sales volume, to see how much the project's result moves.
FIN-04.Scenario analysis: A comparison of a project's results under several complete sets of assumptions, such as best case, expected case and worst case.
FIN-04.Modified internal rate of return: A version of internal rate of return that assumes cash inflows are reinvested at a realistic rate, such as the firm's cost of capital.
FIN-04.Real options analysis: A method that puts a value on the flexibility to expand, delay or abandon a project later as conditions change.
FIN-04.Monte Carlo simulation: A computer model that runs a project thousands of times with randomly varied inputs to show the range of likely outcomes.
FIN-04.Equivalent annual annuity: A project's net present value converted into an equal yearly amount, so projects with different lifespans can be compared fairly.

FIN-05.Accountant: Records, checks and reports an organization's financial activity and often prepares its tax returns.
FIN-05.Financial advisor: Helps individuals plan their money, including saving, investing, insurance and retirement.
FIN-05.Bank teller: Works at a bank counter handling deposits, withdrawals and other everyday transactions for customers.
FIN-05.Banker: Works for a bank, opening accounts, arranging loans and looking after customer relationships or running a branch.
FIN-05.Stockbroker or trader: A stockbroker buys and sells investments on behalf of clients. A trader buys and sells to profit from price changes.
FIN-05.Financial analyst: Studies companies, industries and financial data to recommend investments or guide business decisions.
FIN-05.Loan officer: Reviews loan applications at a bank or lender and helps decide whether a borrower qualifies.
FIN-05.Insurance agent: Sells insurance policies and helps customers choose coverage that fits their needs.
FIN-05.Bookkeeper: Records a business's daily transactions, such as sales, purchases and payments, and keeps its accounts up to date.
FIN-05.Financial manager: Oversees an organization's finances, including budgets, reports and plans for meeting its long-term money goals.
FIN-05.Auditor: Examines an organization's financial records to check that they are accurate and follow the rules.
FIN-05.Investment banker: Helps companies raise money by issuing stocks and bonds and advises them when they merge with or buy other companies.
FIN-05.Tax preparer: Fills out and files tax returns for individuals or businesses and looks for deductions they are allowed to claim.
FIN-05.Chief financial officer: The top executive in charge of a company's finances, responsible for planning, reporting and managing financial risk.
FIN-05.Portfolio manager: Decides which investments to buy and sell for a fund or for clients, aiming to meet set return and risk goals.
FIN-05.Mortgage broker: A go-between who matches home buyers with lenders and helps arrange the home loan.
FIN-05.Actuary: Uses math and statistics to measure the likelihood and cost of events such as accidents or deaths, so insurers can set prices.
FIN-05.Underwriter: Evaluates the risk of insuring a person or approving a loan and decides whether to accept it and on what terms.
FIN-05.Controller: The head of a company's accounting department, responsible for its records, financial reports and internal controls.
FIN-05.Treasurer: Manages an organization's cash, borrowing and investments so it always has the money it needs.
FIN-05.Credit analyst: Studies the finances of a person or business to judge how likely they are to repay a loan.
FIN-05.Budget analyst: Helps an organization plan its spending, reviews budget requests and tracks whether spending stays on plan.
FIN-05.Risk manager: Identifies what could cause an organization financial loss and plans ways to reduce, avoid or insure against it.
FIN-05.Venture capitalist: Invests money in young, fast-growing companies in return for part ownership, hoping some become very valuable.
FIN-05.Payroll or accounting clerk: A payroll clerk calculates and issues employee pay. An accounting clerk enters and checks routine financial records.
FIN-05.Claims adjuster: Investigates insurance claims to decide whether the policy covers the loss and how much the insurer should pay.
FIN-05.Compliance officer: Makes sure a financial firm and its employees follow laws, regulations and the firm's own policies.
FIN-05.Financial examiner: Reviews banks and other financial institutions, often for a government regulator, to check they are sound and follow the law.
FIN-05.Collections agent: Contacts people and businesses with overdue debts and arranges for them to pay.
FIN-05.Quantitative analyst: Builds mathematical and computer models to price investments, measure risk and guide trading decisions.
FIN-05.Credit counselor: Advises people who are struggling with debt, helping them build a budget and a plan to repay what they owe.

FIN-06.Present value: What a future sum of money is worth today, given the interest it could earn in the meantime.
FIN-06.Future value: What a sum of money today will grow to by a later date at a given interest rate.
FIN-06.Interest rate: The percentage that money earns or costs per period. It is the growth rate used to move values forward or back in time.
FIN-06.Compound interest: Interest earned on both the original amount and the interest already added, so the balance grows faster each period.
FIN-06.Simple interest: Interest calculated only on the original amount, so the same dollar amount is earned every period.
FIN-06.Principal: The original amount of money invested or borrowed, before any interest is added.
FIN-06.Number of periods: How many years, months or other intervals the money is invested or borrowed for. More periods mean more growth.
FIN-06.Annuity: A series of equal payments made at regular intervals, such as monthly loan payments or yearly deposits.
FIN-06.Discount rate: The interest rate used to convert future money into its value today. A higher rate makes future money worth less now.
FIN-06.Payment: The equal amount paid or received each period in an annuity or loan calculation.
FIN-06.Rule of 72: A shortcut for estimating how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate as a percentage.
FIN-06.Inflation: The general rise in prices over time. It means a dollar in the future will buy less than a dollar does today.
FIN-06.Cash flow: Money received or paid at a particular point in time. Each one is valued according to when it happens.
FIN-06.Net present value: The present value of all future cash inflows minus the present value of the costs. It shows the gain in today's dollars.
FIN-06.Perpetuity: A stream of equal payments that continues forever. Its present value is the payment divided by the interest rate.
FIN-06.Opportunity cost: The return you give up by not choosing the next best use of your money. It is why money received later is worth less.
FIN-06.Annual percentage rate: The yearly interest rate on a loan as stated, without counting the effect of compounding within the year.
FIN-06.Lump sum: A single amount paid or received all at once, as opposed to a series of payments.
FIN-06.Amortization: Paying off a loan through equal regular payments. Each payment covers the interest due and reduces part of the balance.
FIN-06.Effective annual rate: The true yearly rate earned or paid once compounding within the year is counted. It is higher than the stated rate when interest compounds more than once a year.
FIN-06.Compounding frequency: How often interest is added to the balance, such as yearly, monthly or daily. More frequent compounding means slightly faster growth.
FIN-06.Continuous compounding: The mathematical limit where interest is added constantly instead of at set intervals. It gives the most growth possible for a stated rate.
FIN-06.Internal rate of return: The interest rate at which the present value of an investment's cash inflows equals its cost.

ACC-04.FIFO: First in, first out. An inventory method that assumes the oldest items bought are the first ones sold, so ending inventory holds the newest costs.
ACC-04.LIFO: Last in, first out. An inventory method that assumes the newest items bought are sold first, so ending inventory holds the oldest costs.
ACC-04.Straight-line depreciation: Spreads an asset's cost, minus its expected resale value, evenly over its useful life, so the expense is the same every year.
ACC-04.Weighted average cost: An inventory method that divides the total cost of goods available for sale by the units available, giving one average cost per unit.
ACC-04.Declining balance: A depreciation method that applies a fixed percentage to the asset's remaining book value each year, so the expense is largest early on.
ACC-04.Units of production: A depreciation method based on use. The asset's cost, minus its expected resale value, is spread over the total units it should produce, and each year is charged for what it made.
ACC-04.Specific identification: An inventory method that tracks the actual cost of each individual item sold. It suits unique, high-value goods such as cars or jewelry.
ACC-04.Sum-of-the-years-digits: An accelerated depreciation method that uses a shrinking fraction each year. For a 5-year asset the fractions are 5/15, then 4/15 and so on, because 1+2+3+4+5 is 15.
ACC-04.Accelerated depreciation: Any depreciation method that charges more of an asset's cost in its early years and less in its later years.
ACC-04.MACRS: The Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System, the depreciation system U.S. businesses use on federal tax returns. It sets fixed recovery periods by type of asset.
ACC-04.Lower of cost or market: A rule that inventory must be reported at whichever is lower, what it cost or what it is currently worth, so losses in value are recognized.
ACC-04.Retail inventory method: A way for stores to estimate the cost of ending inventory by applying the ratio of cost to retail price to the retail value of goods on hand.
ACC-04.Gross profit method: A way to estimate ending inventory by using the business's usual gross profit percentage to work out the cost of goods sold.
ACC-04.Standard costing: Valuing inventory at a planned cost per unit set in advance, then tracking the differences between planned and actual costs.

ACC-05.Matching principle: Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped to earn, so profit for the period is measured fairly.
ACC-05.Accrual basis: Revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, not when cash actually changes hands.
ACC-05.Revenue recognition: Revenue is recorded when the business has earned it by delivering the goods or services, even if payment comes later.
ACC-05.Historical cost: Assets are recorded at the price actually paid for them, not at what they might be worth today.
ACC-05.Consistency: A business uses the same accounting methods from one period to the next, so its results can be compared over time.
ACC-05.Materiality: An item matters if leaving it out or misstating it could change a reader's decision. Trivial amounts may be handled in the simplest way.
ACC-05.Conservatism: When in doubt, choose the option least likely to overstate assets or profit. Expected losses are recorded early, gains only when certain.
ACC-05.Going concern: The assumption that the business will keep operating into the foreseeable future and will not be forced to close and sell off its assets.
ACC-05.Full disclosure: Financial statements and their notes must include all information that could affect a reader's understanding of the business.
ACC-05.Business entity: The assumption that a business's finances are kept separate from the personal finances of its owners and from other businesses.
ACC-05.Time period: The assumption that a business's life can be divided into equal periods, such as months, quarters and years, for reporting.
ACC-05.Comparability: Financial information should be prepared so readers can compare one company with another and one year with the next.
ACC-05.Reliability: Information should be accurate, complete and free from bias, so readers can depend on it.
ACC-05.Relevance: Information should be capable of making a difference to the decisions of the people who read the statements.
ACC-05.Monetary unit: The assumption that only things measurable in money are recorded, using one stable currency such as the dollar.
ACC-05.Objectivity: Records should be based on evidence that can be checked, such as receipts and invoices, not on personal opinion.
ACC-05.Regularity: From a commonly taught list of ten generally accepted accounting principles: accountants follow the established rules and regulations as a matter of course.
ACC-05.Sincerity: From a commonly taught list of ten generally accepted accounting principles: the accountant aims to give an honest and accurate picture of the company's finances.
ACC-05.Non-compensation: From a commonly taught list of ten generally accepted accounting principles: report both good and bad results in full, without offsetting debts against assets or expenses against revenue.
ACC-05.Utmost good faith: From a commonly taught list of ten generally accepted accounting principles: everyone involved in a transaction is assumed to be acting honestly.
ACC-05.Timeliness: Information should reach readers soon enough to be useful for their decisions. Old information loses value.
ACC-05.Understandability: Information should be presented clearly enough that a reader with reasonable business knowledge can follow it.
ACC-05.Substance over form: Transactions are reported according to their real economic effect, not just their legal wording.
ACC-05.Cost-benefit constraint: The benefit of reporting a piece of information should be greater than the cost of gathering and presenting it.

ACC-06.Invoice: A bill a seller sends to a buyer listing the goods or services supplied, the amount owed and when payment is due.
ACC-06.Receipt: A written record given to a customer as proof that payment was made for a purchase.
ACC-06.Check: A written order telling a bank to pay a stated amount from the writer's account. The stub or copy is the record of the payment.
ACC-06.Purchase order: A form a buyer sends to a supplier to order goods, stating the items, quantities and agreed prices.
ACC-06.Bank statement: The bank's periodic list of every deposit, withdrawal and fee on an account. It is used to check the business's own cash records.
ACC-06.Time card: A record of the hours an employee worked, used to calculate wages.
ACC-06.Deposit slip: A form listing the cash and checks put into a bank account, kept as proof of the deposit.
ACC-06.Contract: A legally binding written agreement, such as a lease or loan agreement, that sets out amounts and terms to be recorded.
ACC-06.Cash register tape: The printed or electronic record of every sale rung up on a register during the day, used to record total cash sales.
ACC-06.Memorandum: A short written note explaining a transaction when no other document exists, such as an owner taking supplies for personal use.
ACC-06.Credit memo: A form a seller issues to reduce what a customer owes, usually because goods were returned or a price was lowered.
ACC-06.Packing slip: A list sent with a shipment showing what the package contains, so the buyer can check it against the order.
ACC-06.Voucher: An internal form that authorizes a payment and gathers the supporting documents, such as a slip for cash taken from petty cash.
ACC-06.Pay stub: The statement given with a paycheck showing an employee's earnings and deductions. It supports the payroll entry.
ACC-06.Expense report: A form an employee submits listing business costs they paid personally, with receipts, so they can be repaid.
ACC-06.Sales order: A seller's internal record of a customer's order, showing what was requested before the goods are shipped and billed.
ACC-06.Debit memo: A form a buyer sends to a supplier to say it is reducing the amount it owes, usually for returned or damaged goods.
ACC-06.Receiving report: A form filled in when goods arrive, recording what was actually delivered and its condition.
ACC-06.Purchase requisition: An internal request from a department asking the purchasing staff to buy certain goods. It comes before the purchase order.
ACC-06.Bill of lading: A document issued by a carrier listing the goods it has taken for shipment. It serves as a receipt and a contract for the transport.
ACC-06.Remittance advice: A note sent along with a payment telling the seller which invoice is being paid and how much.

ACC-07.Operating activities: The section showing cash from the day-to-day business, such as money collected from customers and paid to suppliers and staff.
ACC-07.Investing activities: The section showing cash spent on, or received from, long-term assets and investments, such as buying equipment.
ACC-07.Financing activities: The section showing cash exchanged with lenders and owners, such as borrowing, repaying loans, issuing stock and paying dividends.
ACC-07.Net income: The profit from the income statement. Under the indirect method it is the starting line of the operating section.
ACC-07.Net change in cash: The total of the three sections. It shows how much the cash balance rose or fell during the period.
ACC-07.Depreciation: An expense that reduced net income without any cash leaving the business, so it is added back in the operating section.
ACC-07.Dividends paid: Cash paid out to shareholders from profits. It is a cash outflow in the financing section.
ACC-07.Capital expenditures: Cash spent on long-lived assets such as buildings and equipment. It is an outflow in the investing section.
ACC-07.Change in accounts receivable: An adjustment in the operating section. A rise in what customers owe means some sales have not yet been collected in cash, so it is subtracted.
ACC-07.Change in inventory: An adjustment in the operating section. A rise in inventory means cash was spent on goods not yet sold, so it is subtracted.
ACC-07.Change in accounts payable: An adjustment in the operating section. A rise in what is owed to suppliers means some costs have not yet been paid in cash, so it is added.
ACC-07.Proceeds from borrowing: Cash received from taking out loans or issuing bonds. It is an inflow in the financing section.
ACC-07.Repayment of debt: Cash used to pay back the principal of loans or bonds. It is an outflow in the financing section.
ACC-07.Issuance of stock: Cash received from selling new shares to investors. It is an inflow in the financing section.
ACC-07.Sale of equipment or other assets: Cash received from selling long-lived assets the business no longer needs. It is an inflow in the investing section.
ACC-07.Purchase or sale of investments: Cash paid to buy, or received from selling, stocks, bonds and similar holdings in other organizations. It belongs in the investing section.
ACC-07.Cash received from customers: Under the direct method, the first line of the operating section, showing the actual cash collected from sales.
ACC-07.Cash paid to suppliers and employees: Under the direct method, an operating outflow showing the actual cash paid for inventory, services and wages.
ACC-07.Changes in working capital: The combined adjustment for movements in current assets and current liabilities, such as receivables, inventory and payables.
ACC-07.Stock repurchases: Cash a company spends buying back its own shares from investors. It is an outflow in the financing section.
ACC-07.Beginning and ending cash balances: The lines at the bottom that add the period's net change in cash to the opening balance to reach the closing balance.
ACC-07.Interest and taxes paid: The actual cash paid for interest and income taxes in the period, shown in the operating section or as a separate disclosure.
ACC-07.Gain or loss on sale of assets: An adjustment in the operating section. A gain is subtracted and a loss added back, because the sale's cash appears under investing.
ACC-07.Noncash investing and financing activiti: A separate note for major deals that used no cash, such as buying land by issuing stock or a long-term note.

PFL-04.Income tax: A tax on the money a person earns from wages, a business or investments. It is charged by the federal government and most states.
PFL-04.Sales tax: A percentage added to the price of goods, and some services, at the checkout. States and local governments set the rate.
PFL-04.Property tax: A yearly tax based on the value of land and buildings a person owns. It mainly funds local services such as schools.
PFL-04.Payroll tax: Taxes taken out of wages to fund Social Security and Medicare. Employers pay a matching amount.
PFL-04.Capital gains tax: A tax on the profit made when an investment or property is sold for more than it cost.
PFL-04.Excise tax: A tax on specific goods such as gasoline, tobacco or alcohol. It is usually built into the price.
PFL-04.Local income tax: An income tax charged by some cities, counties or school districts on top of federal and state income tax.
PFL-04.Estate tax: A tax on the total property a person leaves behind at death, paid out of the estate before heirs receive it. It applies only to large estates.
PFL-04.Inheritance tax: A tax some states charge the person who receives money or property from someone who has died.
PFL-04.Luxury tax: A tax on expensive, non-essential goods such as high-priced cars, boats or jewelry.
PFL-04.Personal property tax: A yearly tax some states and localities charge on movable belongings, most often cars and other vehicles.
PFL-04.Gift tax: A federal tax that can apply to a person who gives away money or property above set limits. The giver, not the receiver, is responsible.
PFL-04.Self-employment tax: The Social Security and Medicare tax paid by people who work for themselves. They pay both the employee and employer shares.
PFL-04.Value-added tax: A sales-type tax collected at each stage of production and included in the final price. It is common outside the United States.
PFL-04.Use tax: A tax owed on goods bought without paying sales tax, such as from an out-of-state seller, and then used in your home state.
PFL-04.Tariff: A tax on goods brought in from other countries. Importers pay it, and it often reaches households through higher prices.
PFL-04.Hotel occupancy tax: A tax added to the bill for a hotel room or other short-term lodging, charged by a city, county or state.
PFL-04.Alternative minimum tax: A separate federal income tax calculation that limits certain tax breaks so that higher earners pay at least a minimum amount.
PFL-04.Real estate transfer tax: A one-time tax charged by some states and localities when ownership of a house or land passes from seller to buyer.

PFL-05.Housing: Rent or mortgage payments for the place you live. For most households it is the largest single budget item.
PFL-05.Food: Groceries and meals eaten out. Groceries are a need, while restaurant meals are usually counted as a want.
PFL-05.Transportation: The cost of getting around, such as a car payment, fuel, repairs or bus and train fares.
PFL-05.Utilities: Regular bills for services to the home, such as electricity, water, heating, internet and phone.
PFL-05.Savings: Money set aside for emergencies and future goals. Putting this in the budget first is called paying yourself first.
PFL-05.Entertainment: Spending on fun, such as movies, streaming services, hobbies and trips. It is a want, so it is easy to cut when money is tight.
PFL-05.Insurance: Premiums paid for coverage such as car, health, renters or life insurance.
PFL-05.Clothing: Money for clothes and shoes. Basic clothing is a need, but much clothing spending is a want.
PFL-05.Health care: Out-of-pocket medical costs such as doctor visits, prescriptions and dental care that insurance does not pay.
PFL-05.Debt payments: Money owed each month on student loans, credit cards and other borrowing, apart from a mortgage or car loan budgeted elsewhere.
PFL-05.Education: School costs such as tuition, books, supplies and fees.
PFL-05.Taxes: Taxes not already taken out of a paycheck, such as property tax or extra income tax owed at filing time.
PFL-05.Needs and wants: The two broad groups a budget sorts spending into. Needs are essentials such as housing and food, and wants are extras you could do without.
PFL-05.Charitable giving: Money donated to charities, religious organizations or other causes.
PFL-05.Child care: What parents pay for daycare, babysitters or after-school care.
PFL-05.Retirement contributions: Money put into a retirement account, such as a 401(k) or IRA (individual retirement account), for use later in life.
PFL-05.Personal care: Spending on grooming and hygiene, such as haircuts, toiletries and cosmetics.
PFL-05.Gifts: Money set aside for birthday, holiday and other presents. Planning for it avoids a surprise at busy times of year.
PFL-05.Household supplies and maintenance: The cost of keeping a home running, such as cleaning products, furniture and repairs.
PFL-05.Miscellaneous: A small catch-all amount for minor or unexpected costs that do not fit any other category.
PFL-05.Pets: The cost of caring for an animal, including food, supplies and veterinary bills.
PFL-05.Child support or alimony: Court-ordered payments to a former partner. Child support helps pay for raising a child, and alimony supports a former spouse.

PFL-06.Identity theft: Someone steals your personal details, such as your Social Security number, and uses them to open accounts or borrow in your name.
PFL-06.Phishing: Fake emails, texts or calls that pretend to be from a trusted company to trick you into giving up passwords or account numbers.
PFL-06.Credit card fraud: Someone uses your card or card number without permission to make purchases or withdraw money.
PFL-06.Ponzi scheme: A fake investment that pays earlier investors with money from newer ones instead of real profits. It collapses when new money dries up.
PFL-06.Pyramid scheme: A setup where people pay to join and earn mainly by recruiting others, not by selling a real product. Most who join lose money.
PFL-06.Online shopping scam: A fake store or listing takes your payment and then sends nothing, or sends something worthless.
PFL-06.Imposter scam: A caller or message pretends to be from the government, a bank or another trusted body and demands money or personal details.
PFL-06.Romance scam: A scammer builds a fake online relationship, gains the victim's trust and then asks for money.
PFL-06.Skimming: A hidden device on a card reader, such as at an ATM or gas pump, copies your card details when you swipe or insert the card.
PFL-06.Investment fraud: Lying to investors about an investment, for example by promising high returns with no risk, in order to take their money.
PFL-06.Telemarketing fraud: Scams carried out by phone, where callers use pressure and false promises to get payments or personal details.
PFL-06.Fake check scam: A scammer sends a counterfeit check and asks you to send part of the money back. When the check bounces, you lose what you sent.
PFL-06.Pump and dump: Fraudsters spread hype to push up the price of a cheap stock they own, then sell at the top. The price crashes and other buyers lose.
PFL-06.Advance fee scam: The victim is promised a large sum, loan or prize but must first pay a fee. After the fee is paid, the promised money never arrives.
PFL-06.Lottery scam: You are told you won a prize or lottery you never entered, but must pay taxes or fees up front to collect it.
PFL-06.Charity scam: A fake charity, often appearing after a disaster, collects donations that the scammers keep for themselves.
PFL-06.Grandparent scam: A caller pretends to be a grandchild or other relative in urgent trouble and begs an older person to send money right away.
PFL-06.Job scam: A fake job offer used to collect upfront fees or personal and bank details from people looking for work.
PFL-06.Cryptocurrency scam: Fraud involving digital currency, such as fake coins or trading platforms. Crypto payments are very hard to reverse.
PFL-06.Gift card scam: A scammer insists you pay a supposed debt or fee by buying gift cards and reading out the numbers. Real organizations do not do this.
PFL-06.Spoofing: Faking a caller ID, email address or website so a message appears to come from a source you trust.
PFL-06.Tech support scam: A pop-up or caller falsely claims your computer has a virus, then charges for fake repairs or asks for remote access to it.
PFL-06.Affinity fraud: An investment scam aimed at members of a close group, such as a church or ethnic community, that exploits their trust in each other.
PFL-06.Rental scam: A fake listing for a home the scammer does not own or control, used to collect a deposit or first month's rent.
PFL-06.Credit repair scam: A company charges upfront fees and falsely promises to erase accurate negative information from your credit report or wipe out your debts.
PFL-06.Foreclosure rescue scam: A company promises, for a fee, to save the home of someone behind on a mortgage. It takes the money and does little or nothing.
PFL-06.Pharming: Malicious code or a hacked internet setting silently redirects you from a real website to a fake copy that steals your login details.
PFL-06.Money mule scam: Criminals recruit someone to receive and pass along stolen money through their own account. The recruit can face legal trouble.

PFL-07.Truth in Lending Act: Requires lenders to state the cost of credit clearly, including the annual percentage rate (APR), so borrowers can compare offers.
PFL-07.Fair Credit Reporting Act: Sets rules for credit bureaus. It gives people the right to see their credit reports and to dispute errors in them.
PFL-07.Dodd-Frank Act: Passed in 2010 after the financial crisis, it tightened rules on banks and created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
PFL-07.Sarbanes-Oxley Act: Passed in 2002 after accounting scandals such as Enron, it makes public company executives personally certify their financial reports.
PFL-07.Fair Debt Collection Practices Act: Bans debt collectors from using abusive, deceptive or unfair tactics, such as threats or calls at unreasonable hours.
PFL-07.Equal Credit Opportunity Act: Makes it illegal for lenders to discriminate against credit applicants because of race, sex, religion, age, marital status and similar factors.
PFL-07.CARD Act: The Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure Act of 2009. It limits surprise rate increases and fees and restricts card offers to people under 21.
PFL-07.Securities Act of 1933: Requires companies selling new stocks or bonds to the public to register them and give investors truthful information in a prospectus.
PFL-07.Securities Exchange Act of 1934: Created the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and regulates the trading of securities after they are first issued.
PFL-07.Glass-Steagall Act: A 1933 law that separated commercial banking from investment banking and created federal deposit insurance. The separation was repealed in 1999.
PFL-07.Fair Credit Billing Act: Lets credit card users dispute billing errors and limits how much they must pay for unauthorized charges.
PFL-07.Consumer Credit Protection Act: A 1968 umbrella law for consumer credit. It includes the Truth in Lending Act and limits how much of a worker's pay can be garnished.
PFL-07.Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act: Requires financial institutions to explain how they share customers' personal information and to protect that data.
PFL-07.Electronic Fund Transfer Act: Protects people who use debit cards, ATMs and electronic transfers, including limits on losses from unauthorized transactions reported promptly.
PFL-07.Truth in Savings Act: Requires banks to disclose the fees and the annual percentage yield (APY) on deposit accounts so savers can compare them.
PFL-07.Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act: Requires home buyers to be told their closing costs in advance and bans kickbacks among the companies involved in a home sale.
PFL-07.Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Ac: A 2003 law that gives people a free yearly credit report from each bureau and adds protections against identity theft, such as fraud alerts.
PFL-07.Investment Company Act of 1940: Regulates mutual funds and similar investment companies, requiring them to register and to disclose their finances and policies.
PFL-07.Investment Advisers Act of 1940: Requires people paid to give investment advice to register and to put their clients' interests first.
PFL-07.Securities Investor Protection Act: Created the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC), which helps return customers' cash and securities if a brokerage firm fails.
PFL-07.Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act: Adds extra disclosures and bans certain abusive terms on high-cost home loans, to protect borrowers from predatory lending.
PFL-07.Military Lending Act: Caps the interest rate and bans certain unfair terms on many loans made to active-duty service members and their families.
PFL-07.Credit Repair Organizations Act: Bars credit repair companies from making false promises and from charging customers before the promised work is done.

BNK-01.Checking account: An account for everyday money. You can deposit pay and spend from it by debit card, check or online payment.
BNK-01.Savings account: An account for money you do not need right away. The bank pays you interest on the balance.
BNK-01.Loans: Money the bank lends that you repay over time with interest, such as a car loan, personal loan or line of credit.
BNK-01.Mortgage: A long-term loan used to buy a home. The home is the security, so the lender can take it if the loan is not repaid.
BNK-01.Credit card: A card that lets you borrow up to a set limit for purchases. Interest is charged on any balance not paid off by the due date.
BNK-01.Debit card: A card that pays for purchases by taking the money straight out of your checking account.
BNK-01.ATM: An automated teller machine, where you can withdraw cash, make deposits and check your balance without a teller.
BNK-01.Online banking: Access to your accounts through a website or app to check balances, pay bills, move money and deposit checks.
BNK-01.Certificate of deposit: A deposit you agree to leave for a fixed term in return for a fixed interest rate, usually higher than a savings account pays.
BNK-01.Deposit accounts: The general service of holding customers' money safely in accounts such as checking and savings.
BNK-01.Money market account: A savings-type account that often pays a higher rate, may need a larger balance and may allow a limited number of checks.
BNK-01.Safe deposit box: A locked box in the bank's vault that you rent to store valuables and documents. Its contents are not covered by deposit insurance.
BNK-01.Direct deposit: An electronic payment, such as a paycheck or tax refund, sent straight into your account with no paper check.
BNK-01.Checks: Paper forms you fill in and sign to order the bank to pay someone from your checking account.
BNK-01.Money transfers: Moving money electronically between your own accounts or to another person's account.
BNK-01.Wire transfer: A fast electronic transfer sent directly from one bank to another, often for large or international payments, usually for a fee.
BNK-01.Cashiers check or money order: Prepaid payment documents. A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, and a money order is a similar prepaid slip for smaller sums.
BNK-01.Overdraft protection: A service that covers a payment when your checking balance is too low, often by moving money from a linked savings account.
BNK-01.Investment services: Help with investing and planning, such as retirement accounts, brokerage accounts and advice from a financial advisor.
BNK-01.Business accounts: Checking, savings and payment services designed for companies, including the ability to accept card payments.
BNK-01.Notary services: A bank employee who is a notary public witnesses signatures on important documents and confirms the signer's identity.
BNK-01.Currency exchange: Swapping one country's money for another's, for example buying euros with dollars before a trip.
BNK-01.Trust services: Managing money and property on behalf of someone else under a legal arrangement called a trust, or handling a person's estate.
BNK-01.Custodial account: An account an adult opens and manages for a child. The money belongs to the child, who takes control on reaching adulthood.

BNK-02.Federal funds rate target: The range the Fed sets for the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. Moving it pushes other interest rates up or down.
BNK-02.Open market operations: The Fed buying and selling government securities. Buying adds money to the banking system, and selling takes money out.
BNK-02.Discount rate: The interest rate the Fed charges banks that borrow from it directly through its lending desk, called the discount window.
BNK-02.Reserve requirements: The share of customer deposits banks must hold back and not lend out. The Fed can change it, though it currently sets it at zero.
BNK-02.Quantitative easing: Large-scale purchases of longer-term bonds by the Fed to push down long-term interest rates when short-term rates are already very low.
BNK-02.Interest on reserve balances: The rate the Fed pays banks on money they keep at the Fed. Banks have little reason to lend for less, so it helps steer market rates.
BNK-02.Forward guidance: Public statements by the Fed about where it expects to take interest rates, which shape what businesses and investors do today.
BNK-02.Quantitative tightening: The Fed shrinking its bond holdings, usually by letting bonds mature without replacing them. This takes money out of the financial system.
BNK-02.Moral suasion: The Fed using persuasion and public pressure, without formal rules, to influence how banks behave.
BNK-02.Margin requirements: The Fed's rule on how much of a stock purchase an investor must pay with their own money, which limits buying with borrowed funds.
BNK-02.Overnight reverse repurchase agreements: The Fed sells securities to financial firms overnight and buys them back the next day, paying interest. This sets a floor under short-term rates.
BNK-02.Emergency lending facilities: Special loan programs the Fed opens during a crisis so that credit keeps flowing. This is its role as lender of last resort.
BNK-02.Standing repo facility: A permanent program through which eligible firms can borrow cash from the Fed overnight against safe securities. It helps cap short-term rates.
BNK-02.Central bank liquidity swaps: Agreements in which the Fed temporarily trades dollars for another central bank's currency, so foreign banks can get dollars in a crisis.
BNK-02.Term deposit facility: A program that lets banks place money at the Fed for a set term and earn interest, which temporarily drains reserves from the banking system.

BNK-03.Debit card: A card that pays by pulling the money directly from your checking account, usually within a day or two.
BNK-03.Credit card: A card that pays with money borrowed from the card issuer. You repay it later, with interest if you do not pay in full.
BNK-03.Check: A signed paper order telling your bank to pay a stated amount from your account to the person or business named.
BNK-03.Mobile wallet: An app such as Apple Pay or Google Pay that stores your card details on a phone so you can pay by holding it near a reader.
BNK-03.Payment app: An app such as Venmo, Zelle or PayPal that sends money from your account or card to another person, often within minutes.
BNK-03.Online bill pay: A bank or biller service that sends payments electronically from your account, either one at a time or automatically each month.
BNK-03.Contactless payment: Paying by tapping a card or phone on a reader. A chip sends the payment details by short-range radio signal.
BNK-03.Prepaid card: A card loaded with money in advance. You can spend only what is on it, and it is not linked to a bank account or a credit line.
BNK-03.Money order: A prepaid paper payment bought for a set amount at a post office, bank or store. The receiver knows the funds are already paid.
BNK-03.ACH transfer: An electronic payment between bank accounts over the Automated Clearing House network, used for direct deposit and automatic bill payments.
BNK-03.Wire transfer: An electronic transfer sent directly from one bank to another. It is fast and hard to reverse, and banks usually charge a fee.
BNK-03.Cashiers check: A check drawn on the bank's own funds after you pay the bank the amount. Sellers trust it for large purchases.
BNK-03.Cryptocurrency: Digital money such as Bitcoin, sent directly between users over a computer network without a bank in the middle.
BNK-03.Buy now pay later: A service that splits a purchase into a few installments, often interest-free if paid on time. It is a form of short-term borrowing.
BNK-03.Certified check: A personal check that the bank has stamped to confirm the money is in your account and has been set aside to pay it.
BNK-03.Travelers check: A prepaid check for a fixed amount that can be replaced if lost or stolen. It was once common for travel and is now rarely used.
BNK-03.Barter: Trading goods or services directly for other goods or services, with no money changing hands.
BNK-03.Store credit or rewards points: Value held with a retailer or card program, earned from returns or past spending, that can be used in place of money for a purchase.

BNK-04.Overdraft fee: Charged when you spend more than is in your account and the bank covers the payment anyway.
BNK-04.Monthly maintenance fee: A regular charge just for having the account. Banks often waive it if you keep a set balance or use direct deposit.
BNK-04.ATM fee: Charged for using a cash machine outside your bank's network. The machine's owner may add its own charge as well.
BNK-04.Minimum balance fee: Charged when the money in your account drops below the amount the bank requires you to keep.
BNK-04.NSF fee: A non-sufficient funds fee, charged when a check or payment is rejected and returned because the account did not hold enough money.
BNK-04.Wire transfer fee: Charged for sending, and sometimes receiving, money by wire transfer between banks.
BNK-04.Foreign transaction fee: A percentage charged when you use your card abroad or pay in another currency.
BNK-04.Stop payment fee: Charged when you ask the bank to block a check or scheduled payment before it goes through.
BNK-04.Paper statement fee: Charged for having account statements printed and mailed instead of receiving them online.
BNK-04.Card replacement fee: Charged for issuing a new debit card when yours is lost or damaged, especially if you want it rushed.
BNK-04.Inactivity fee: Charged when an account has had no deposits or withdrawals for a long period.
BNK-04.Cashiers check fee: Charged for issuing a cashier's check, a guaranteed check drawn on the bank's own funds.
BNK-04.Check printing fee: The cost of ordering a new supply of paper checks for your account.
BNK-04.Excess withdrawal fee: Charged when you take money out of a savings account more times in a month than the bank allows.
BNK-04.Account closing fee: Charged if you close an account soon after opening it, often within the first few months.
BNK-04.Returned deposited item fee: Charged when a check you deposited bounces because the person who wrote it did not have enough money.
BNK-04.Overdraft protection transfer fee: Charged when the bank automatically moves money from a linked account to cover a payment your checking balance could not.

INV-01.Market order: An instruction to buy or sell right away at the best price currently available. It is almost sure to fill, but the price is not guaranteed.
INV-01.Limit order: An instruction to buy at no more than, or sell at no less than, a price you set. It may never fill if the market does not reach that price.
INV-01.Stop order: An order that becomes a market order once the stock reaches a set price. A stop-loss sells a falling stock to limit further loss.
INV-01.Stop-limit order: An order that becomes a limit order, not a market order, once the stock reaches a set stop price. It controls price but may not fill.
INV-01.Day order: An order that is cancelled automatically if it has not been filled by the end of the trading day.
INV-01.Good-til-canceled order: An order that stays open across trading days until it is filled or the investor cancels it, up to a limit set by the broker.
INV-01.Trailing stop order: A stop order whose trigger price follows the stock up by a set amount or percentage, locking in gains while limiting losses.
INV-01.Fill or kill: An order that must be filled completely and immediately, or else the whole order is cancelled.
INV-01.All or none: An order that must be filled in full or not at all. Unlike fill or kill, it can wait until enough shares are available.
INV-01.Immediate or cancel: An order to fill as much as possible right away. Any part that cannot be filled at once is cancelled.
INV-01.Market on close: An order to buy or sell at the market price as near as possible to the end of the trading day.
INV-01.Market on open: An order to buy or sell at the market price when trading opens for the day.
INV-01.Good-til-date order: An order that stays open until a date the investor chooses, unless it is filled or cancelled first.
INV-01.One-cancels-the-other order: Two linked orders placed together. As soon as one is filled, the other is cancelled automatically.
INV-01.Limit on close: An order to trade at the closing price, but only if that price is at or better than the limit the investor sets.
INV-01.Conditional order: An order that is sent to the market only when a condition the investor sets is met, such as another stock or an index reaching a level.

INV-02.Market risk: The chance that the whole market falls and drags most investments down with it. Diversifying does not remove it.
INV-02.Inflation risk: The chance that prices rise faster than your investment grows, so your money buys less than before.
INV-02.Interest rate risk: The chance that interest rates rise and make existing bonds, which pay the older, lower rate, fall in price.
INV-02.Loss of principal: The chance of getting back less than you originally put in, or nothing at all.
INV-02.Credit risk: The chance that a bond issuer or other borrower fails to pay the interest or repay the money owed.
INV-02.Liquidity risk: The chance that you cannot sell an investment quickly without accepting a lower price.
INV-02.Business risk: The chance that one particular company does badly or fails. Spreading money across many companies reduces it.
INV-02.Economic risk: The chance that a recession or other downturn in the economy hurts company profits and investment values.
INV-02.Currency risk: The chance that a change in exchange rates reduces the value of a foreign investment when it is converted back to your own money.
INV-02.Political risk: The chance that government instability, conflict or a sudden change of policy in a country harms investments there.
INV-02.Financial risk: The chance that a company's heavy borrowing leaves it unable to meet its debt payments, hurting its investors.
INV-02.Concentration risk: The danger of holding too much in one stock, industry or kind of asset, so a single setback does serious damage.
INV-02.Reinvestment risk: The chance that interest or principal paid back to you can only be reinvested at a lower rate than before.
INV-02.Regulatory risk: The chance that a new law, rule or tax change hurts the value of an investment.
INV-02.Industry risk: The chance that an entire industry suffers, for example from new technology or falling demand, hurting every company in it.
INV-02.Horizon risk: The chance that you need your money sooner than planned and must sell at a bad time.
INV-02.Fraud risk: The chance that an investment turns out to be a scam or that the people running it lie about it.
INV-02.Call risk: The chance that a bond issuer repays the bond early, usually when rates have fallen, ending the investor's higher interest payments.
INV-02.Longevity risk: The chance of living longer than your retirement savings last.
INV-02.Event risk: The chance that a single unexpected event, such as a takeover, lawsuit or disaster, suddenly cuts the value of an investment.
INV-02.Prepayment risk: The chance that borrowers pay off loans early, as with mortgages behind a security, so investors get money back sooner and earn less interest.
INV-02.Sequence of returns risk: The danger that big market losses come early in retirement, when withdrawals are being made, shrinking savings much faster.

INV-03.S&P 500: Tracks about 500 of the largest U.S. companies, weighted by size. It is the most common yardstick for the U.S. stock market.
INV-03.Dow Jones Industrial Average: Tracks 30 large, well-known U.S. companies. It is one of the oldest indexes and is weighted by share price, not company size.
INV-03.Nasdaq Composite: Tracks nearly all the stocks listed on the Nasdaq exchange, several thousand in total, with a heavy share of technology companies.
INV-03.Russell 2000: Tracks about 2,000 smaller U.S. companies. It is the usual measure of how small-company stocks are doing.
INV-03.FTSE 100: Tracks the 100 largest companies listed on the London Stock Exchange. It is the main index for the United Kingdom.
INV-03.Nikkei 225: Tracks 225 large companies on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. It is the best-known index for Japan.
INV-03.Nasdaq-100: Tracks 100 of the largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, dominated by big technology names.
INV-03.Wilshire 5000: Built to cover nearly every publicly traded U.S. company, making it one of the broadest measures of the U.S. market.
INV-03.DAX: Tracks 40 of the largest companies on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange. It is the main index for Germany.
INV-03.Hang Seng: Tracks the largest companies on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It is the main index for Hong Kong.
INV-03.NYSE Composite: Tracks all the common stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
INV-03.Russell 1000 or 3000: The Russell 3000 covers about 3,000 of the largest U.S. companies, nearly the whole market. The Russell 1000 is the largest 1,000 of them.
INV-03.S&P MidCap 400 or SmallCap 600: Two indexes that follow U.S. companies below the S&P 500 in size: 400 medium-sized companies and 600 small ones.
INV-03.CAC 40: Tracks 40 of the largest companies listed on the Paris stock exchange. It is the main index for France.
INV-03.MSCI EAFE: Tracks large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the U.S. and Canada. EAFE stands for Europe, Australasia and the Far East.
INV-03.Shanghai Composite: Tracks all the stocks listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange. It is a main index for mainland China.
INV-03.MSCI World: Tracks large and mid-sized companies across developed countries around the world, including the United States.
INV-03.MSCI Emerging Markets: Tracks large and mid-sized companies in developing economies such as China, India and Brazil.
INV-03.Euro Stoxx 50: Tracks 50 of the largest companies in countries that use the euro.
INV-03.S&P/TSX Composite: Tracks the largest companies on the Toronto Stock Exchange. It is the main index for Canada.
INV-03.Sensex: Tracks 30 large companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange. It is one of India's two main indexes.
INV-03.Nifty 50: Tracks 50 large companies on the National Stock Exchange of India. It is one of India's two main indexes.
